Impingement Syndrome
Introduction
The term impingement syndrome was coined by Neer; however, the concept of abrasion
between the undersurface of the acromion and the bursal side of the rotator cuff was first
proposed by Meyer in 1931.
This contact between the undersurface of the acromion and the greater tuberosity was felt to
be pathologic, leading to bursitis and rotator cuff abrasion.
Neer described the anterior acromial spur and proposed its removal for the management of
impingement.
Neer described three stages of impingement.
Stage I: inflammation and edema in the rotator cuff
Stage II: tendinitis of the rotator cuff
Stage III: rotator cuff tearing with ossification of the coracoacromial ligament.
Acromioplasty increased in incidence by 254% during the 2000s.
The role of the acromion in impingement is a subject of debate.

Introduction
The term impingement syndrome was initially popularized by Neer;1 however, the
concept of abrasion between the undersurface of the acromion and the bursal side of
the rotator cuff was first proposed by Meyer2 in 1931. This abrasion was felt to be
pathologic, leading to subacromial bursitis and pain and was proposed to lead to rotator
cuff tears. Meyer2 first proposed that this impingement between the rotator cuff and the
acromion led to mechanical attrition of the rotator cuff and was the cause of rotator cuff
tears. Currently, it is known as the extrinsic cause of rotator tears.
Radical acromionectomies were popular in the 1960s; however, in the 1970s, Neer3
published a series of papers outlining the anatomy of the spur, an enthesophyte at the
coracoacromial ligament insertion into the anterior undersurface of the acromion,
proposing that all but the anterior acromion were “innocent.” He proposed the removal
of this anterior spur and the attached coracoacromial ligament for management.3 Neer3
also described the stages of impingement syndrome, from stage I to stage III, beginning

Patient Evaluation
Impingement syndrome is detected via a patient history, physical examination, and
imaging studies, which largely are nonspecific. Originally, impingement syndrome was
described as anterolateral shoulder pain and pain with abduction. These symptoms
largely overlap with those of other shoulder pathology, such as subacromial bursitis,
labral tears, biceps tendinitis, rotator cuff tears, and acromioclavicular joint pathology.
Neer3 first proposed using the Neer sign for the evaluation of impingement syndrome, in
which the shoulder is passively elevated in the frontal plane. As elevation increases, the
greater tuberosity moves under the acromion and produces pain; however, as elevation
continues, the greater tuberosity rotates posterior to the acromion and the pain
improves. The Neer test—in which a local anesthetic is injected in the subacromial space,
and the pain then subsides—also was proposed. The Hawkins-Kennedy test involves
abducting the shoulder to 90° and then passively internally rotating the shoulder to
induce contact between the greater tuberosity and the acromion, causing pain.5 These
tests may be positive for various shoulder conditions, leading to a high sensitivity but
less than 50% specificity reported in a large systematic review.6 Initial imaging studies
involve a shoulder radiographic series that includes a supraspinatus outlet view to
evaluate acromial morphology. This view is highly positional and technique dependent,
with small changes in angulation leading to apparent changes in acromial shape and
size.
Acromial Morphology
The acromion and coracoacromial ligament form a hemispheric arch that fits the curvature of
the humeral head.
Codman7 and Depalma8 believed that the anterior spur was an osseous extension of the
coracoacromial ligament and not pathologic.

Bigliani et al9 first classified acromia into three types: flat, curved, or hooked.
Hooked acromia were thought to lead to a higher incidence of rotator cuff tears. In the initial
series by Bigliani et al,9 40% of the acromia were hooked, with 70% of all rotator cuff tears
present in this group.
Critical shoulder angle: also known as the lateral acromial angle; measured as the angle
between the superior and inferior bony margins of the glenoid and the lateralmost aspect of
the acromion.
Multiple studies have shown that the critical shoulder angle is associated with an increased
incidence of rotator cuff tears.

Acromial Morphology
The articulation between the undersurface of the acromion/coracoacromial ligament
and the superior humerus is thought to be a normal articulation. It was described by
Codman7 as a hemisphere that matched the curvature of the superior humerus. This
description matched the contour similarly referred to by Depalma8 as the superior
humeral articulation (Figure 1). This hemispheric contour includes the proposed anterior
spur of the acromion, which can be observed as an osseous extension of the
coracoacromial ligament—an enthesophyte—that still matches the contour of the
superior humeral head. The coracoacromial ligament ossifies; however, the overall
shape of the coracoacromial arch is unchanged.

Another radiographic parameter proposed to be associated with rotator cuff tears is the
lateral acromial angle12 or the critical shoulder angle13 (Figure 3). This angle
incorporates the glenoid and acromial tilt in the frontal plane. It is measured as the angle
between the superior and inferior bony margins of the glenoid and the most lateral
aspect of the acromion. Many studies have proposed that lower angles result in less
space available for the rotator cuff to move before contacting the acromion. Multiple

incidence of rotator cuff tears.12-15 Other studies have proposed that rather than

of the deltoid, causing shear across the glenohumeral joint and requiring the
supraspinatus to apply increased force to counteract this and predisposing the shoulder
to rotator cuff tears. A cadaver model biomechanical study showed that, as the critical
shoulder angle increased, shear increased across the glenohumeral joint, requiring
additional supraspinatus loading to stabilize the joint in the coronal plane.16 Subsequent
quantitative finite element modeling studies have confirmed that larger critical shoulder
angles require additional rotator cuff activity to stabilize the glenohumeral joint.17 This
increased load within the rotator cuff for stability is thought to predispose the rotator
cuff to failure rather than the mechanical abrasion of the rotator cuff. A correlation has
been reported between lower critical shoulder angles and the development of
glenohumeral osteoarthritis,13,18 thought to be caused by increased compressive forces
across the glenohumeral joint from the more horizontal/compressive force vector of the
deltoid in patients with a low critical shoulder angle.
Although these two classification systems differ, they both propose that acromial
morphology may be pathologic, leading to abnormal mechanical abrasion or rotator cuff
stress distribution as an extrinsic cause of rotator cuff tears (Resources 1 and 2).

Secondary Impingement
Pathologic impingement between the humerus and the acromion may be the result of other
conditions.
Chronic rotator cuff tears with superior migration of the humeral head may lead to pathologic
articulation between the humerus and the acromion.
Scapular dyskinesia leads to scapular protraction and anterior tilt, causing impingement of the
humerus and the acromion at lower than normal levels of elevation.

Abnormal impingement between the humerus and the undersurface of the acromion
may be the result of other conditions, termed secondary impingement. The patient
history and physical examination should be tailored to closely evaluate for these other

humerus and the acromion.20,21 Another cause of secondary impingement is scapular
dyskinesia, in which the acromion is excessively protracted and tilted anteriorly,22
possibly leading to abnormal impingement between the humerus and the acromion.
Lastly, posteroinferior capsular tightness has been proposed to cause anterosuperior
translation of the humeral head with flexion, leading to impingement with the
acromion22 (Figure 4).

Management
Largely nonsurgical via anti-inflammatory medications, physical therapy to address any
scapular dyskinesia and improve rotator cuff force couples, and corticosteroid injections (CSIs)
Initial studies showed better patient outcomes with arthroscopic acromioplasty than with
nonsurgical management, leading to a large increase in the number of acromioplasties.
A large systematic review of multiple level I studies showed no difference in outcomes
between surgical acromioplasty and nonsurgical management.
Whether surgical acromioplasty is of any benefit or whether postsurgical physical therapy
should be credited for improvement after this procedure remains unclear.
From an economic/reimbursement perspective, Medicare and many other payors no longer

Management
The original description of the stages of impingement syndrome by Neer28 advocated for
nonsurgical management of impingement for stage I and stage II with inflammatory
changes but without bony changes or rotator cuff tearing. Despite this finding,
acromioplasty is one of the most commonly performed orthopaedic procedures and
continues to increase in incidence.4 Nonsurgical management largely consists of physical
therapy, activity modifications, and anti-inflammatory medications. The adjunct of CSIs
also may be beneficial.

Initial studies showed that patients had better outcomes with surgical treatment;25
however, most level I evidence, including a large systematic review, has shown that
surgical and nonsurgical management afford effective pain relief with no substantial
benefit to surgical management.30-33 Surgery is effective above and beyond the placebo
effect; however, physical therapy appears to be equally effective. A prospective,
randomized trial compared subacromial decompression, physical therapy, and a
detuned laser placebo.30 The subacromial decompression and physical therapy groups
had similar success rates, both of which were substantially higher than those of the
placebo group. This trial showed that regardless of the treatment option selected,
surgical or nonsurgical, the outcome will be improved compared with placebo.
The definitive question is whether surgical management provides any benefit or if the
physical therapy performed postoperatively leads to the successful outcome. This
question was answered in a prospective, randomized study comparing subacromial
decompression with acromioplasty versus physical therapy, including only patients in
whom at least 3 months of nonsurgical treatment—including physical therapy and CSI—
failed.32 Many believed that additional physical therapy would not be beneficial in
patients in whom physical therapy failed and would show a clear indication for surgical
management; however, no substantial difference was observed between the
subacromial decompression group and the group that continued physical therapy.
Economics have pushed treatment toward nonsurgical management, with studies
demonstrating reduced overall costs compared with surgical management.32 In 2012,
the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services ceased payment for arthroscopic
subacromial decompression as a standalone procedure. Increasing numbers of payors
are no longer reimbursing for isolated subacromial decompression given the lack of
evidence for its use and no clear benefit over nonsurgical management.

Conclusions
Impingement syndrome has been one of the most discussed and commonly diagnosed
pathologies of the shoulder. Impingement syndrome was originally described by Neer1
as a framework in which to understand the development of rotator cuff disease and
guide management. Radiographic studies by Bigliani et al9 and Moor et al13 resulted in
radiographic classification systems that showed a correlation with rotator cuff tears;
however, these remain correlations without any definitive causation. These morphologic
changes of the acromion have been shown to be age-related, as have rotator cuff tears,
because of their age-related decrease in vascularity. Considering factors such as the age-
related correlation, the bilateral nature of the disease, and the common tear locations,
strong evidence suggests an intrinsic degeneration process for most degenerative
rotator cuff tears. Nonsurgical management also has been shown to be as effective and
less expensive than surgical subacromial decompression with acromioplasty. If bony
impingement caused by acromial spurring was the cause, physical therapy alone, with
no modification of the bony architecture, would not be expected to lead to outcomes
similar to those of acromioplasty. Given the relatively nonspecific patient history and
physical examination findings that lead to the diagnosis of impingement syndrome, the
underlying diagnosis likely always been some other pathology, such as bursitis,
tendinitis, or rotator cuff tearing. The authors of many studies in the literature concur
that impingement syndrome caused by an acromial spur, as proposed by Neer, is not
the primary process that explains the origin of most degenerative rotator cuff tears.

Pathophysiology
Calcific tendinitis remains relatively poorly understood, but patients present with acute
calcium phosphate crystal (hydroxyapatite) deposition within the rotator cuff tendon,
most commonly the supraspinatus tendon. A historic study by Bosworth34 estimated
that the prevalence of calcific tendinitis in the working population is 2.7%, with 35% of
those individuals being asymptomatic. The exact etiology of calcific tendinitis remains
unclear; however, it may be an exquisitely painful pathology. Calcific tendinitis is most
commonly observed in middle-aged patients aged 30 to 60 years. Women are affected
more commonly than men.35 An association with endocrine disorders exists, and calcific
tendinitis tends to develop at an earlier age in patients with an associated endocrine
disorder, with a longer symptom duration and a higher rate of surgical management.
Less is known about calcific tendinitis than other pathologies about the shoulder, which
may be partly because it generally is self-limited, with spontaneous resolution. Current
understanding is that this process is cell mediated, with three stages: precalcific, calcific,
and postcalcific.36 The precalcific stage generally is pain free, and fibrocartilaginous
metaplasia of tenocytes into chondrocytes predominantly occurs in less vascular areas
of the tendon. The calcific stage represents the stage of calcium deposition, in which
calcium depositions within matrix vesicles coalesce to form foci of calcification. Often,

Evaluation
A thorough patient history and physical examination are necessary, bearing in mind any
previous endocrine disorders and the duration of symptoms. Patients may present with
crepitus, reduced range of motion, scapular dyskinesia, or impingement signs on
physical examination. Given the prevalence of asymptomatic calcium deposition
observed on radiographs,34 radiographic presence is not diagnostic, and other
pathologies should be considered simultaneously. The calcification from calcific
tendinitis typically occurs 1.5 to 2 cm from the tendon insertion. MRI or CT may be
helpful to evaluate for concomitant disorders rather than to evaluate for calcific
tendinitis. Calcium deposits appear hypointense on all MRI sequences and may not be
readily observed within the tendon on MRI.
Ultrasonography has been used for the evaluation and management of calcific tendinitis.
In skilled hands, ultrasonography can be used to quantify and localize the extent of
calcium deposition. Calcium deposits appear hyperechoic on ultrasonography, which can
be used for diagnosis and for localization during needle decompression (known as
barbotage) or injection.
Management
Most management remains nonsurgical, including anti-inflammatories, physical therapy, and
CSIs.

Diagnostic imaging begins with plain radiographs, which allow for evaluation for other
conditions that may contribute to shoulder pain, such as acromioclavicular joint

Nonsurgical Management
Most patients with a symptomatic atraumatic rotator cuff tear undergo some form of
nonsurgical treatment before surgical treatment is considered. The shoulder is an
incredibly dynamic joint given its uniquely mobile connection to the appendicular
skeleton through the periscapular muscles and the acromioclavicular joint. Poor

surgical treatment and undergo nonsurgical treatment alone.60 The most important
predictor for success with nonsurgical treatment was the patient’s belief that the
physical therapy would be effective. Those who proceeded with surgical treatment often

Open and Mini-Open Rotator Cuff Repair
Historically, the preferred option for rotator cuff repair was an open approach, which
has become less common with the advent of arthroscopy and improved arthroscopic
tools and implants. Currently, open or mini-open repair typically is performed after
diagnostic arthroscopy to assess for concomitant pathology. A typical open approach
involves the detachment of the anterior head of the deltoid and division of the
anterolateral deltoid raphe, extending from the lateral edge of the acromion no more
than 5 cm to prevent axillary nerve injury. The mini-open approach does not include
detachment of the anterior head and works through the deltoid split alone. The
disadvantage of these approaches is damage to the deltoid. The open approach,
particularly, fell out of favor because release of the deltoid off the acromion may lead to
dysfunction. The original repairs performed via the open and mini-open approaches
were transosseous repairs without anchors. Tunnels were drilled into the greater
tuberosity from the lateral cortex to the rotator cuff footprint, and sutures were passed
through the bone tunnel and the tendon and then tied. Mini-open repair is associated
with a risk of revision or arthrofibrosis twice that of arthroscopic repair.71

Management of Partial-Thickness Tears
Overview
Partial-thickness tears are less understood compared with full-thickness tears.
Patients with a partial-thickness rotator cuff tear often present with pain that began insidiously
rather than weakness, as observed in patients with a full-thickness rotator cuff tear.
MRI studies have shown 20% of asymptomatic individuals to have partial-thickness tears,
whereas cadaver model studies report the incidence of asymptomatic partial-thickness tears
between 13% and 32%.
Grading: grade 1, less than 3 mm or 25% of the tendon insertion from medial to lateral; grade

than 50% of the tendon insertion.

Overview
In general, partial-thickness rotator cuff tears have been studied less and are
understood more poorly than full-thickness rotator cuff tears. Compared with full-
thickness rotator cuff tears, which may be associated with weakness, partial-thickness
rotator cuff tears often are associated with an insidious onset and primarily pain. This
pain may be attributed to other pain generators, such as scapular dyskinesia,
subacromial bursitis, or impingement. Cadaver model studies have estimated a partial-
thickness rotator cuff tear prevalence of 13% to 32%,125,126 whereas MRI studies of
asymptomatic individuals have reported a partial-thickness rotator cuff tear prevalence
of 20%, which was age related.127

Historically, the indication for surgical management has been a rotator cuff tear greater than

Indications
Historically, the indication for surgical management has been a rotator cuff tear greater
than 50% of the tendon insertion; this has been based on a single retrospective study of
65 patients with a partial-thickness rotator cuff tear.134 Thirty-two of the patients
underwent arthroscopic acromioplasty alone, and 33 of the patients underwent
arthroscopic acromioplasty followed by mini-open rotator cuff repair. The repair group
had higher University of California–Los Angeles Shoulder Scores at follow-up of 2 years

been supported by cadaver model biomechanical studies, which have shown that an
increase in strain in surrounding tissues occurs only after 50% of the tendon has been
released.136 Therefore, although 50% has been used historically as the threshold for
surgical management, this value is largely arbitrary and other patient factors should be
considered before proceeding with surgical management.

Arthroscopic Repair
In considering a repair of a partial-thickness rotator cuff tear, two options are available:
in situ transtendinous repair and completion of the partial-thickness tear to a full-
thickness tear with repair. Completion of the rotator cuff tear makes the procedure
technically simpler; however, proponents of transtendinous repair argue that leaving the
portion of the tendon intact creates a stronger bone-tendon interface. Biomechanical
studies have shown that transtendinous repairs are associated with a higher load to
failure compared with repair performed after tear completion.144 Repair types are based
on tear characteristics and involve the use of the same constructs as those for repair of
full-thickness rotator cuff tears.
Many studies have shown that transtendinous repair and tear completion with repair
lead to excellent outcomes, with 80% to 95% of tendons healed.145 Four randomized
controlled trials compared transtendinous repair and tear completion with repair.146-149
None of the studies reported a difference in outcomes between the two techniques. A
study that performed postoperative MRI showed a healed tendon in 98.2% of the
patients in the transtendinous repair group and 94.2% of the patients in the tear
completion group.149

Graft Augmentation
Although more heavily studied in patients with a full-thickness rotator cuff tear, various
supplemental grafts, including human dermal allograft, fascia lata autograft, xenografts,
and synthetic patches, have been increasingly used in repair of partial-thickness rotator
cuff tears. Currently, data are lacking because of a dearth of well-controlled studies;
however, a recent meta-analysis by Bailey et al150 assessed the outcomes of graft
augmentation to rotator cuff repair. The authors reported that graft augmentation led to
lower re-tear rates and higher ASES scores compared with rotator cuff repair alone. The
authors also showed that xenografts tended to perform poorest of the augments. These
findings show promise for graft augmentation in rotator cuff repair; however, cautious
optimism must remain pending additional well-controlled studies.

for the use of bioinductive collagen patches has increased. These grafts are placed
without formal repair of the rotator cuff tear. In the largest study to date, which included
a cohort of 33 patients, the use of a collagen graft led to improved ASES and Constant
assessment scores at a follow-up of 12 months.151 In addition, postoperative MRI
revealed a decrease in rotator cuff tear size in 23 of 32 tears, complete tear healing in 8
of 32 tears, and no change in 1 of 32 tears. Early data are promising: however, this
technique requires additional investigation.
